title: Strange Printer
statement: A printer starts with a blank line as long as `s` and works in strokes. One stroke picks a single letter and any contiguous range of positions, and writes that letter on every position of the range, hiding whatever was printed there before. Return the smallest number of strokes after which the line reads exactly `s`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every stroke sequence explodes quickly. Look at a range `s[left..right]` and ask how its last letter `s[right]` gets printed. Either it gets a stroke of its own, or it shares one with an earlier equal letter `s[mid]`: the stroke that prints `s[mid]` can simply be stretched to reach `right` for free, and whatever lies strictly between `mid` and `right` is printed on top of it afterwards. Both choices depend only on smaller ranges, which is interval DP.

## Approach

1. `dp[left][right]` is the fewest strokes for `s[left..right]`; one letter needs one stroke.
2. Fill rows from `left = n - 1` down to `0`, and `right` upward, so every shorter range is ready.
3. Start with `dp[left][right - 1] + 1`: print the rest, then give `s[right]` its own stroke.
4. For every `mid` with `s[mid] === s[right]`, stretch that stroke: cost `dp[left][mid] + inside`, where `inside` is the cost of the gap `mid + 1..right - 1` (0 when empty).
5. Return `dp[0][n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aaabbb"`. Row `left = 0`: `dp[0][0] = 1`; `dp[0][1]` and `dp[0][2]` stay `1` because each new `a` matches the letter just before it with an empty gap. `dp[0][3] = dp[0][2] + 1 = 2` (no earlier `b`). For `right = 4` and `5`, `mid = right - 1` is a `b` with an empty gap, so the cost stays `dp[0][4] = dp[0][5] = 2`. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) ranges, each tries O(n) split points.
- Space: O(n²) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- Fill order matters: `dp[mid + 1][right - 1]` belongs to a later row, so `left` must run backwards.
- The gap between `mid` and `right` can be empty; its cost is 0, not 1.
- Splitting into two independent halves (`dp[left][mid] + dp[mid + 1][right]`) alone misses the shared stroke and overcounts, as in `"aba"`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `dp[left][right]` | fewest strokes to print `s[left..right]` |
| `left`, `right` | ends of the current range |
| `mid` | earlier position whose stroke may be stretched to `right` |
| `inside` | strokes needed for the gap between `mid` and `right` |

narration.2: Remember the length of the string.
narration.3: dp[left][right] will hold the fewest strokes for the piece s[left..right].
narration.5: Go through start positions from the right so every shorter range below is already solved.
narration.6: A single letter always takes exactly one stroke.
narration.7: Grow the range one letter at a time to the right.
narration.8: Default plan: print the rest of the range, then give s[right] a stroke of its own.
narration.9: Look for an earlier position mid whose stroke could be stretched to cover right.
narration.10: Only a position showing the same letter as s[right] can share its stroke.
narration.11: Different letter: this mid cannot help, so skip it.
narration.13: Cost of the gap strictly between mid and right, which is zero when the gap is empty.
narration.14: Stretch the stroke of s[mid] to right and print the gap on top; keep the cheaper plan.
narration.18: The whole string is the range from 0 to n - 1.
